title: Stratospheric ozone depletion: a key driver of recent precipitation trends in South Eastern South America
problem: The cause of the large 20th-century wetting trend in South Eastern South America has been unclear, as regional surface impacts directly attributable to stratospheric ozone depletion had not been identified and distinguished from the effects of increasing greenhouse gases.
method: This study uses a multi-model approach, contrasting pairs of climate model integrations run with and without stratospheric ozone depletion while keeping other forcings identical, to isolate and attribute its specific impact on recent precipitation trends in South Eastern South America.
task: The task is to assess the impact of stratospheric ozone depletion on recent precipitation trends in South Eastern South America by analyzing simulations from six different climate models to attribute the cause of the region's observed wetting.
innovation: This paper uses a multi-model analysis to demonstrate that stratospheric ozone depletion was a key driver of the observed wetting trend in South Eastern South America (1960-1999), with an impact as large as, or possibly larger than, that of increasing greenhouse gases.

kg_extraction_triplets.paragraph: Abstract On a hemispheric scale, it is now well established that stratospheric ozone depletion has been the principal driver of externally forced atmospheric circulation changes south of the Equator in the last decades of the 20th Century. The impact of ozone depletion has been felt over the entire hemisphere, as reflected in the poleward drift of the midlatitude jet, the southward expansion of the summertime Hadley cell and accompanying precipitation trends deep into the subtropics. On a regional scale, however, surface impacts directly attributable to ozone depletion have yet to be identified. In this paper we focus on South Eastern South America (SESA), a region that has exhibited one of the largest wetting trends during the 20th Century. We study the impact of ozone depletion on SESA precipitation using output from 6 different climate models, spanning a wide range of complexity. In all cases we contrast pairs of model integrations with and without ozone depletion, but with all other forcings identically specified. This allows for unambiguous attribution of the computed precipitation trends. All 6 climate models consistently reveal that stratospheric ozone depletion results in a significant wetting of SESA over the period 1960–1999. Taken as a whole, these model results strongly suggest that the impact of ozone depletion on SESA precipitation has been as large as, and quite possibly larger than, the one caused by increasing greenhouse gases over the same period.

It has been established that SESA interannual variability is primarily driven by a strong El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) teleconnection (e.g., Ropelewski and Halpert 1996), and by the influence of the Indian Ocean Dipole (Chan et al. 2008) and the Southern Annular Mode (Zhou et al. 2001; Silvestri and Vera 2003), albeit to a lesser extent.

a. CAM3 time-slice integrations. The simplest model integrations we have analyzed were performed with the Community Atmospheric Model, version 3 (CAM3), documented in Collins et al. (2006). For these experiments, CAM3 was run with T42 horizontal resolution and 26 hybrid vertical levels, only 8 of which are located above 100 hPa.
The model top being at 2.2 hPa, CAM3 can be referred to as a low-top model, in which the stratospheric circulation is poorly resolved.

The second set of model integrations were carried out with the Canadian Middle Atmosphere Model (CMAM), a coupled atmosphere-ocean model that extends so as to encompass the entire middle atmosphere, as detailed in Scinocca et al. From transient runs with an atmosphere-only model (CAM3), we next consider transient runs with a coupled atmosphere-ocean model (with land surface and sea-ice components), the Community Climate System Model, version 4 (CCSM4). This is one of the models used by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR) to produce simulations for the Climate Model Intercomparison Project, Phase 5 (CMIP5). For the output analyzed here, the resolution of the model atmosphere was 1.25° longitude by 0.9° latitude (called '1° version'), with 26 vertical levels (a low-top model); this was coupled to the Parallel Ocean Program version 2 (POP2), as described by Smith et al. b. CMAM The version of CMAM used here is quite similar to the one described in Sect. 2.2.1 above. There is one key difference: this version was integrated with interactive stratospheric chemistry. Because of the computational cost associated with the chemistry component, the horizontal resolution was reduced to T31, with the model top at 0.00081 hPa. Compared to WACCM, these CMAM integrations have the advantage of being fully coupled to the NCOM 1.3 ocean general circulation model. This model configuration, and the associated integrations described below, are documented in McLandress et al. (2010). The chemistry-coupled version of CMAM is, in terms of complexity, the most comprehensive of the models we have analyzed.
